children.text: Romance as a genre was traditionally a masculine genre, focusing on the heroic and chivalric journey of the knight, who would win the hand of the woman. The hero would typically perform heroic deeds in the woman's honour. Following the 18th Century and Jane Austen, the romance genre would re-emerge as a feminine genre.

The evolution of the romance genre is often attributed to Jane Austen. She was originally writing what was known as the "novel of manners" where the main character should be an ideal heroine who does not have to undertake character growth. When she wrote

Austen turned the focus of the romance novel into introspection. Her characters began to change for the better, learning from each other and growing together. They would actively re-evaluate their opinions of each other, and not remain set in their ways.

children.text: presented society with two fundamentally flawed characters, who both learned from their behaviour, and adjusted accordingly.

Elizabeth Bennett was full of pride, to her own detriment. She failed to realise how improperly her family was acting towards members of society, and that it may have contributed to her sister's lack of a proposal from Mr Bingley.

Mr Darcy was full of prejudice towards Elizabeth's family, as they were lower class. He was also prejudiced towards Elizabeth herself, deeming her "tolerable, but not pretty enough to tempt me." Mr Darcy later ate his own words, when Elizabeth quoted them as a rejection of his proposal.

The two characters had to learn to put aside their pride and prejudice, and act respectfully towards one another, and slowly, their character development unfolded into what is considered one of the best romance novels in existence.
